subLevels.instruction: Fill in the directions (−1 pt per wrong placement)
subLevels.reveal: German Ost and West carry particular historical weight — decades after the reunification of the two Germanies in 1990, people from each side are still sometimes called Ossis and Wessis. The yearning some Ossis feel for their old way of life even has its own word: Ostalgie.

subLevels.german: „Im Westen nichts Neues“ ist ein Buch über den Ersten Weltkrieg.

hints.hint: The English title has the same gist as, but is a more poetic translation of, the original German title.
Japan was one of die Alliierten during the Ersten Weltkrieg but was one of die Achsenmächte during the Zweiten Weltkrieg.
The book is by Erich Maria Remarque.

subLevels.reveal: Well done — this was a genuine toughie. Erich Maria Remarque's quietly devastating anti-war novel was banned and burned by the Nazis.

subLevels.german: Wien und Salzburg sind Städte in Österreich.
subLevels.reveal: Österreich literally means "eastern realm", so named because for a time it formed the eastern boundary of the Holy Roman Empire. Which is ironic because Austria's often confused with Australia, which means "southern land"! Austrian tourist shops have leaned into this with merch like this:
subLevels.revealImageAlt: A yellow diamond-shaped road warning sign in the style of an Australian wildlife crossing sign with the classic kangaroo silhouette, but with the added words "No kangaroos in Austria".

subLevels.german: Der Weihnachtsmann bringt Kindern Geschenke wie Santa Claus, aber er lebt nicht am Nordpol und er hat keine Rentiere.

hints.hint: We previously discussed how Tier is cognate with "deer" in English. What's a kind of deer associated with 🎅?

subLevels.reveal: The Weihnachtsmann, literally "Christmas man", is the main Christmastime gift-bringer im Norden (more Protestant), but im Süden (more Catholic) it's the Christkind ("Christ child"). As if this wasn't enough, there's also Sankt Nikolaus, who visits earlier on December 6, and also brings small gifts!

subLevels.german: Frohe Weihnachten und ein frohes neues Jahr!

hints.hint: This is a greeting used during the Weihnachtszeit.

subLevels.reveal: 🎄🎊 Frohe means "joyful" or "glad" and is distantly related to the English word "frolic". Though not everyone is jumping for joy when the family comes round!

hints.hint: Same wish, different holiday — also about Jesus.

subLevels.reveal: German and English are unique in their use of a word derived from "east" for Easter, from the pagan name for the month of April, which possibly celebrated a dawn goddess named "Ēostre". Romance, Celtic, and other Germanic languages use a word derived from Greek/Latin "Pascha" (as in Passover) instead.

hints.hint: suchen ~ the English word "seek", but wir suchen for a similar English verb here.

subLevels.reveal: German Ei 🥚 sounds like English "eye", and "eye" in German is Auge 👁️, which has a g like in "egg". Both languages actually started out much closer to what German has now, but English went down some complicated etymological paths and wound up essentially swapping the two.

subLevels.german: Karfreitag ist zwei Tage vor Ostern.

hints.hint: If Vater ~ "father", then vor ~ ? Add a two-letter prefix to get the correct translation.

subLevels.reveal: Karfreitag literally means "Sorrowful Friday". Kar has the same root as "care" — to care for someone is to experience sorrow and anxiety for them. Heavy stuff!

subLevels.german: Am Karfreitag ist Fleisch verboten — kein Huhn, kein Schwein. Aber Fisch ist erlaubt.

hints.hint: We call the Huhn something else, but we still use a cognate of this word for the female of this animal.
erlaubt is the opposite of verboten. Both have direct cognates in English!

subLevels.reveal:
Among the "fish" allowed were beaver and, later, capybara. They live in water, so they're technically fish, right??

Historically these Lenten restrictions were lifted on Easter Sunday, hence the extremely practical Hungarian and Estonian name for Easter — "Meat-Taking Day" ("húsvét" / "lihavõtted")! Forget the resurrection — meat's back on the menu, boys!

subLevels.german: Was war zuerst da, das Huhn oder das Ei?

hints.hint: zuerst is a prefix + erst, which we saw earlier this level in Ersten Weltkrieg.

subLevels.reveal: Let's settle this right here, right now — the first shelled egg evolved around the time reptiles emerged from the water 312 million years ago, while the ancestor to our modern chicken only evolved 4-6 million years ago. The chicken loses by roughly 300 million years. Das Ei kam zuerst!
